nodes.description: The molecular lesion. Salivary neurotoxins of the feeding tick - the holocyclotoxins of Ixodes holocyclus are the only paralysis toxins structurally characterised - act on the motor nerve terminal to reduce the entry of calcium that triggers transmitter release, inhibiting the dependence of release on extracellular calcium rather than disabling the release machinery or the receptor. The effect is temperature dependent.

nodes.description: The integrating step. In health the endplate potential overshoots the threshold to fire the muscle fibre by a wide safety margin; the reduced quantal content narrows that margin until transmission fails at individual endplates and the muscle fibre no longer fires to its nerve. In humans this shows as low-amplitude compound muscle action potentials with normal nerve conduction velocities and normal sensory studies - a motor, presynaptic picture.

nodes.description: When the paralysis reaches the respiratory muscles it causes neuromuscular respiratory failure, the mechanism of death in untreated or late-recognised cases.

evidence.snippet: It typically presents as an acute ascending paralysis occurring a few days after tick attachment and may result in respiratory failure and death.

nodes.description: The exposure is envenomation by a feeding hard tick: the attached tick secretes neurotoxin in its saliva during a blood meal, and symptoms begin a few days after attachment. The toxin dose rises the longer the tick feeds, which is why children, in whom a scalp tick is easily hidden by hair, are most often affected and most severely.

evidence.snippet: Tick paralysis results from inoculation of a toxin from tick salivary glands during a blood meal.

nodes.description: The mainstay and usually the only treatment needed. Finding and removing the attached tick stops delivery of the toxin, and in North American disease is followed by rapid improvement; the whole body, especially the scalp, must be searched. Because the paralysis can mimic Guillain-Barre syndrome, the rule is never to settle on that diagnosis without first searching for a tick.
An unsteady, ataxic gait is characteristically the first manifestation, before overt limb weakness.

evidence.snippet: Tick paralysis is an uncommon, noninfectious, neurologic syndrome characterized by acute ataxia progressing to ascending paralysis.
